topic: Day 2 · Approach to Lower GI Bleeding
speakerTitle: Consultant in Acute Internal Medicine & Gastroenterology
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician and gastroenterologist who runs the hospital's GI bleed pathway and drills every new cohort on the single rule that red blood plus shock is an upper bleed until proven otherwise.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

It is 2am. A 71-year-old man is wheeled in from triage having passed "a whole toilet bowl of blood" twice in the last hour — fresh red clots, no pain. He is on aspirin and apixaban for AF. HR 118, BP 92/54, cool peripheries, GCS 15 but anxious. The triage nurse has written "PR bleed — for colonoscopy in the morning." Two things must happen before anyone thinks about a colonoscope. First, we resuscitate. Second — and this is the trap that catches good doctors — we must prove this is not a brisk upper GI bleed masquerading as blood from below. Get the mental model right and this man survives the night; get it wrong and he arrests during an unprepped colonoscopy that was never going to reach the bleeding point.

1 · 🩸 Definitions — what actually counts as "lower"

Precision here changes the whole work-up. The anatomical dividing line is the ligament of Treitz (the suspensory muscle of the duodenum at the duodeno-jejunal flexure).

  • Lower GI bleeding (LGIB) = bleeding from a source distal to the ligament of Treitz — i.e. small bowel, colon, rectum, or anus. In everyday practice the overwhelming majority are colonic.
  • Upper GI bleeding (UGIB) = bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz — oesophagus, stomach, duodenum.
  • Mid / small-bowel bleeding — jejunum and ileum, beyond the reach of gastroscope and colonoscope; the domain of capsule endoscopy and enteroscopy. Modern nomenclature increasingly splits "lower" into colonic and small-bowel.

The clinical vocabulary of what comes out matters just as much as where it comes from:

TermWhat it looks likeUsual implication
HaematocheziaFresh red or maroon blood / clots per rectumUsually a lower source — BUT a brisk upper bleed can do this (section 3)
MelaenaBlack, tarry, offensive stoolDigested blood — usually an upper source; occasionally right colon / small bowel with slow transit
Maroon stoolDark red, mixedRight colon or distal small bowel
Blood coating stool / on paperBright red streaking, drips after defecationAno-rectal / outlet (haemorrhoids, fissure) — usually minor
Haematochezia is a description, not a diagnosis. It tells you blood came out red — it does not tell you where the tap is.

2 · 🧠 Mechanism first — why lower bleeds behave differently

Understanding two facts explains almost all of LGIB management. First, the colon is a low-pressure, capacious reservoir. Most lower sources are venous, capillary, or small-arterial (a single vasa recta in diverticular disease), and the colon tolerates and often tamponades them. Second, blood is a cathartic — it irritates the gut and speeds transit, so a lower bleed tends to declare itself quickly as red blood rather than sitting long enough to be digested to melaena.

💡 The single most useful fact about LGIB

Roughly 80% of lower GI bleeds stop spontaneously. This is why the default posture is resuscitate, risk-stratify, then investigate electively — not emergency scope for everyone. The minority who keep bleeding or rebleed are the ones who need urgent localisation and haemostasis, and the whole art is spotting them early.

Because most stop on their own, the diagnostic yield of any test falls the longer you wait after bleeding has ceased — you cannot localise a source that is no longer leaking. This tension (stops on its own vs. only findable while active) is the axis around which the entire localisation strategy (session 11) turns.

3 · ⚠️ The crucial trap — a brisk UPPER bleed presenting from below

This is the one idea that, if you take nothing else from this lecture, will save a patient. Around 10–15% of patients presenting with haematochezia are actually bleeding from an UPPER GI source — a duodenal ulcer, varices, or an aorto-enteric fistula pouring out so fast that the blood transits before it can be digested to melaena.

The give-away is the company haematochezia keeps: haemodynamic instability. A truly colonic bleed severe enough to cause shock is uncommon; when a patient has red blood per rectum and is shocked, suspect a massive upper bleed until proven otherwise.

⚠️ Red blood + shock = rule out an upper source FIRST

In the unstable haematochezia patient, do not default to colonoscopy. Consider an upper endoscopy (OGD) first, and/or place a nasogastric tube and aspirate. A bloody or coffee-ground aspirate confirms an upper source; bile without blood makes a high upper source less likely. The ACG 2016 lower GI bleeding guideline explicitly recommends upper endoscopy in patients with haematochezia and haemodynamic instability. Missing a spurting duodenal ulcer while prepping a colon is a classic, preventable death.

💡 The urea clue

An elevated urea (BUN) : creatinine ratio (often quoted >30:1) points to an upper source — blood digested in the small bowel is absorbed as a nitrogen load and raises the urea disproportionately to the creatinine. A rising urea with a normal creatinine in a "PR bleed" should make you reach for the gastroscope.

FeaturePoints UPPERPoints LOWER
Haemodynamic instability with red PR bloodStrongly — brisk upper until excludedPossible but less common
MelaenaTypicalUncommon
Urea:creatinine ratioHigh (>30:1)Normal / proportionate
NG aspirateBlood / coffee groundsClear / bile
HistoryNSAIDs, ulcer, liver disease/varices, prior AAA repairDiverticulosis, prior polypectomy, radiotherapy, painless red blood

4 · 🚑 Stabilisation — resuscitate before you investigate

No test matters until the patient is resuscitated. Run this in parallel with your assessment:

  1. A–B–C, two large-bore cannulae (14–16G), high-flow oxygen, continuous monitoring.
  2. Bloods: FBC (early Hb may be falsely reassuring — it lags), U&E (the urea clue), LFTs, coagulation, group & save / crossmatch, lactate, VBG.
  3. Fluids and blood. Crystalloid to buy time; activate the major haemorrhage protocol if massive/ongoing.
  4. Transfusion threshold — restrictive. Transfuse red cells at a haemoglobin of <7 g/dL (target 7–9) in the haemodynamically stable non-cardiac patient; use a higher trigger (~8 g/dL, target >9) in active massive bleeding or significant cardiovascular disease. This restrictive strategy (extrapolated from Villanueva et al., NEJM 2013) reduced mortality and rebleeding versus liberal transfusion.
  5. Correct coagulopathy: reverse warfarin (PCC + vitamin K) if life-threatening; consider platelet transfusion if <50 with active bleeding; hold/reverse DOACs (idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet/PCC for factor-Xa inhibitors) in life-threatening bleeds. Do not needlessly reverse anticoagulation in a self-limiting minor bleed.
  6. Digital rectal examination and anoscopy — cheap, immediate, and feeds directly into risk scoring.
🎯 The first haemoglobin lies

In acute brisk bleeding the patient loses whole blood — cells and plasma together — so the haemoglobin concentration is initially normal and only falls as haemodilution (endogenous fluid shift and your crystalloid) sets in over hours. A "reassuring" Hb of 132 in a shocked, tachycardic patient is a trap. Trend it, and treat the physiology (HR, BP, lactate, mentation), not a single number.

5 · 🗺️ The localisation strategy — a preview

Once resuscitated and an upper source considered, the question becomes where and how fast. The choice of test is dictated by haemodynamic status and whether bleeding is ongoing (the full modality deep-dive is session 11):

PatientFirst moveRationale
Stable, bleeding settledColonoscopy after bowel prep (next available list; within 24h if high-risk)Diagnostic AND therapeutic; prep improves yield and safety
Unstable / ongoing brisk bleedingCT angiography → catheter angiography ± embolisation; exclude upper sourceNo time to prep; needs active extravasation to localise and treat
Obscure / intermittentRed-cell scintigraphy, repeat colonoscopy, small-bowel work-up (capsule)Most sensitive to slow/intermittent bleeding
The unstable patient with ongoing bleeding goes to CT angiography and interventional radiology — not to an unprepped colonoscopy that cannot see through a colon full of blood.

6 · 📊 Risk stratification — the Oakland score

Not every PR bleed needs admission. The Oakland score (derived and validated in UK cohorts, endorsed by BSG) identifies patients at low risk of adverse outcome who can be safely managed as outpatients — reserving beds and urgent scopes for those who need them.

Oakland variableDetail
AgeIncreasing points with older age
SexMale scores higher
Previous LGIB admissionPrior admission adds points
DRE findingsBlood on rectal examination adds points
Heart rateHigher HR → more points
Systolic blood pressureLower SBP → more points
HaemoglobinThe heaviest-weighted variable — lower Hb → many more points
💡 The number to remember

The Oakland score runs 0–35. A score of ≤8 predicts a ~95% probability of safe discharge — no rebleeding, no transfusion, no intervention, no death. These patients can generally be worked up as outpatients. A high score flags the patient who needs admission, resuscitation, and urgent localisation. Use it to disposition, not to overrule clinical alarm.

7 · ⚖️ Contrast pair — the two faces of haematochezia

Stable minor haematocheziaUnstable haematochezia
StoryBright red streaks, blood on paper, small volume, self-limitingLarge-volume red clots, ongoing, syncope
ObsNormal HR/BP, warmTachycardic, hypotensive, cool
Likely sourceHaemorrhoids, fissure, diverticularRule out brisk upper bleed first; then diverticular / angiodysplasia
OaklandLow (≤8) → outpatient pathwayHigh → admit, resuscitate
First testElective colonoscopy / flexi-sigNG aspirate ± OGD, then CT angiography → IR
TrapAnchoring on "piles" and missing a proximal cancerPrepping a colon while a duodenal ulcer exsanguinates

8 · 🔎 Special situations that change the plan

A handful of contexts should immediately raise or lower your threshold to escalate:

  • The anticoagulated patient — the commonest modern LGIB. Bleeding is often heavier and less likely to self-terminate; balance reversal against the thrombotic indication (mechanical valve, recent stent, VTE) with haematology input. An INR that is supratherapeutic in a warfarinised bleeder needs urgent correction.
  • The elderly, frail patient — poor physiological reserve, silent ischaemia, and polypharmacy (NSAIDs, antiplatelets). A "small" bleed decompensates them fast; the first Hb is even less trustworthy.
  • Recent polypectomy (within 2 weeks) — think post-polypectomy bleeding; this is often endoscopically treatable and the history is the diagnosis (session 10).
  • Prior aortic graft — any GI bleed is an aorto-enteric fistula until proven otherwise; herald bleeds precede catastrophic exsanguination. This is a surgical/vascular emergency, not a colonoscopy.
  • Painless massive bleed in the young adult — consider a Meckel's diverticulum (ectopic gastric mucosa) — a small-bowel source that a colonoscope will never reach.
🎯 Recurrent, self-terminating bleeds

The patient who is admitted three times a year with painless red bleeding that always stops is telling you the source is intermittent — classically angiodysplasia or diverticular disease. Between episodes, tests are often negative; the win is to capture them while bleeding (red-cell scintigraphy or a well-timed CT angiogram) rather than repeating cold colonoscopies. Don't let repeated "normal when settled" scopes lull you into stopping the work-up.

9 · 🧭 The mental model for lower GI bleeding

Hold five sequential questions in your head for every red PR bleed:

  1. Is it really lower? Red blood + shock, or a high urea:creatinine ratio → suspect and exclude an upper source (NG aspirate / OGD) before colonoscopy.
  2. Is the patient stable? Resuscitate first — 2 large cannulae, restrictive transfusion (<7 g/dL; <8 if cardiac/massive), correct coagulopathy.
  3. Is it still bleeding? 80% stop spontaneously — the ongoing/rebleeding minority drive urgency and choice of test.
  4. How high is the risk? Oakland ≤8 → safe for outpatient work-up; high → admit and localise urgently.
  5. Where is it and how do I stop it? Stable → colonoscopy (prep, diagnostic + therapeutic); unstable/ongoing → CT angiography → embolisation; surgery only once localised (sessions 11–12).
☠️ M&M — the "PR bleed for the morning list"

A 68-year-old man presented at midnight with three episodes of fresh red rectal bleeding and clots. HR 110, BP 100/60. He looked "not too bad," the first Hb was 128, and he was booked for a colonoscopy on the next day's list and left on the ward with maintenance fluids. No NG tube was passed; his urea was 14 with a creatinine of 78 — a urea:creatinine ratio nobody flagged. At 4am he had a large melaena-and-red mixed motion, became profoundly hypotensive, and arrested. At post-mortem: a posterior duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery — a massive upper GI bleed that had been transiting so fast it came out red. Lessons: (1) haematochezia with instability is an upper bleed until excluded — the disproportionately high urea screamed it; (2) the first haemoglobin is not reassurance in acute bleeding; (3) an NG aspirate or early OGD, not a colonoscopy "in the morning," was the test he needed; (4) resuscitation and reassessment, not a ward bed and a wait, is the standard of care for the unstable bleeder. The team treated a label ("PR bleed") instead of a physiology (shock).

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. LGIB = bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz; haematochezia describes the blood, it does not localise the source.
  2. Red blood + haemodynamic instability = rule out a brisk UPPER GI bleed first — NG aspirate and/or OGD, and heed a high urea:creatinine ratio.
  3. ~80% of lower GI bleeds stop spontaneously — the default is resuscitate, risk-stratify, then investigate, not scope-for-all.
  4. Resuscitate before you investigate: two large cannulae, restrictive transfusion (Hb <7 g/dL; <8 if cardiac or massive), correct coagulopathy, and never trust the first Hb.
  5. Use the Oakland score: ≤8 → ~95% safe for outpatient management; high score → admit and localise urgently.
  6. Match the test to the patient: stable → prepped colonoscopy; unstable/ongoing → CT angiography → embolisation; surgery only after localisation.

moderatorQs.q: A patient presents with large-volume haematochezia and is hypotensive. The registrar wants an urgent colonoscopy. What is your first move and why?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: My first move is to resuscitate and exclude an upper GI source, not to book a colonoscopy. Around 10–15% of patients with haematochezia are bleeding from above the ligament of Treitz — a brisk duodenal ulcer or varices transiting so fast the blood emerges red — and haemodynamic instability with red PR blood is the classic fingerprint. So: two large-bore cannulae, restrictive transfusion (Hb trigger <7 g/dL, or <8 with cardiac disease/massive bleeding), correct coagulopathy, and pass an NG tube and/or perform an upper endoscopy first (ACG 2016). A bloody or coffee-ground aspirate, or a high urea:creatinine ratio (>30:1), confirms the upper source. An unprepped colonoscopy in a shocked patient sees only blood, cannot reach a proximal upper source, and risks precipitating arrest.

moderatorQs.q: How does the Oakland score change your management, and what threshold matters?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The Oakland score lets me safely avoid admitting low-risk lower GI bleeds. It combines seven variables — age, sex, previous LGIB admission, blood on DRE, heart rate, systolic BP, and (most heavily weighted) haemoglobin — for a total of 0–35. A score of ≤8 predicts roughly a 95% probability of safe discharge: no rebleeding, transfusion, intervention, or death, so these patients can be worked up as outpatients (BSG-endorsed). A high score flags the patient who needs admission, resuscitation, and urgent localisation. It is a disposition tool that formalises the fact that ~80% of these bleeds stop on their own — but it never overrules a clinically alarming patient in front of me.

moderatorQs.q: Why is the first haemoglobin potentially misleading in acute lower GI bleeding, and what should you monitor instead?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because in acute brisk haemorrhage the patient loses whole blood — red cells and plasma in equal proportion — so the concentration of haemoglobin is initially preserved and only falls over hours as endogenous fluid shifts and administered crystalloid haemodilute the remaining cells. A normal or high first Hb in a shocked, tachycardic patient is therefore a dangerous false reassurance. I trend the haemoglobin serially and, more importantly, treat the physiology — heart rate, blood pressure, capillary refill, lactate, urine output, and mental status — alongside estimated blood loss, rather than acting on a single early number.

audienceQs.q: When exactly should I pass an NG tube in someone with rectal bleeding?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Consider it whenever the picture doesn't fit a purely lower bleed — above all in the patient with haematochezia plus haemodynamic instability, or with a disproportionately high urea:creatinine ratio, NSAID or ulcer history, or known varices. The aspirate helps triage: blood or coffee grounds confirms an upper source; bile without blood makes a high upper source less likely (though a non-bloody aspirate never fully excludes a duodenal bleed). In an unstable patient a definitive upper endoscopy is better than relying on the NG tube alone, but the tube is a fast, cheap bedside step while you organise the scope. Don't let a tidy colonoscopy plan blind you to a bleed from above.

audienceQs.q: The patient is on apixaban and aspirin. Do we reverse the anticoagulation straight away?
audienceQs.answerHTML: It depends on severity. In a life-threatening or ongoing massive bleed, yes — reverse: for a factor-Xa inhibitor like apixaban that means andexanet alfa where available, or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC), alongside activating the major haemorrhage protocol; dabigatran is reversed with idarucizumab. In a self-limiting minor bleed in a patient anticoagulated for a strong indication (e.g. mechanical valve, recent VTE), reflex reversal can do more harm than the bleed, so it's a considered, often multidisciplinary decision. Aspirin given for secondary cardiovascular prevention is usually continued; platelet transfusion is reserved for counts <50 with active bleeding or documented dysfunction. Check renal function too — apixaban accumulates in renal impairment, prolonging its effect.

audienceQs.q: If 80% stop on their own, why not just wait and scope everyone electively?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because the 20% who don't stop, plus the fraction hiding a brisk upper bleed, are the ones who die if you wait — and you can't reliably tell them apart on the first look without risk-stratifying and resuscitating. The strategy isn't 'wait for all' or 'scope all'; it's triage: resuscitate everyone, exclude an upper source in the unstable, apply the Oakland score to disposition the low-risk to outpatient colonoscopy, and fast-track the high-risk/ongoing bleeders to urgent localisation (CT angiography → embolisation). Waiting is correct only once you've proven the patient is stable and low-risk. Electively scoping a patient who is quietly still bleeding wastes the diagnostic window and lets a treatable lesion rebleed catastrophically.
